claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel naturally carries an oxide film composed primarily of Fe3O4.
The native oxide film on Q235 steel acts as a protective barrier under room-temperature saline conditions.
The native iron oxide film on Q235 steel is self-healing at room temperature.
Aggressive salts at 700–900 °C chemically flux and destabilize the native iron oxide on Q235 steel.
Thermal-expansion mismatch at 700–900 °C causes the native oxide on Q235 steel to spall.
High-temperature aggressive-salt exposure enhances diffusion and imposes thermal stresses on the Q235 oxide layer.
Loss of oxide continuity exposes Q235 steel and accelerates corrosion.
Q235 steel exposed to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C will lose significantly more mass than Q235 steel exposed to salt at room temperature.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce a spalled or discontinuous oxide layer on Q235 steel.
High-temperature salt exposure will cause pitting and increased corrosion rates in Q235 steel.
A Cr-rich stainless steel with a stable passive film will resist high-temperature salt corrosion better than untreated Q235 steel.
A dense passivation film can provide corrosion resistance in NaCl solution on a CoCrFeNiNb HEA-coated Q235 substrate.
Molten FLiBe exposure at 700 °C can produce substantial mass loss through selective elemental dissolution in a Cr-Mn-Fe-Ni HEA.
Pre-modification with Cr or Nb may produce a more robust passivation film and suppress the proposed Q235 degradation mechanism.
The proposed degradation mechanism should not operate during inert high-temperature exposure.
The proposed mechanism should not operate when the salt lacks sufficient chemical activity to flux the oxide.
A controlled annealing step can standardize the native oxide film on Q235 samples.
The relative contributions of thermal stress and salt chemistry to oxide destabilization on Q235 steel are not yet resolved.
